Muscle weakness and reduced grip strength
- Reduced deep tendon reflexes corresponding to the affected root
- Restricted cervical ROM and muscle spasm
- Symptoms may worsen with cervical movement or compression
**Investigations**
- Cervical X ray for degenerative or bony changes
- MRI for disc pathology nerve root or cord compression
- CT for bony/foraminal abnormalities
- EMG/NCV when nerve involvement needs clarification
- Neurological examination of dermatomes myotomes and reflexes
**Complications**
- Chronic pain
- Persistent sensory deficit
- Motor weakness and muscle wasting
- Loss of hand function
- Reduced work capacity
- Cervical myelopathy in severe cord compression
**Conservative / Medical Management**
- Relative rest and activity modification
- Analgesics/NSAIDs as indicated
- Muscle relaxants in selected cases
- Neuropathic pain medication when appropriate
- Selected use of cervical collar in acute cases
**Physiotherapy Management**
- Pain relief with TENS or thermal modalities when appropriate
- Gentle cervical ROM
- Deep neck flexor and cervical stabilization exercises
- Scapular stabilization and upper limb strengthening
- Postural and ergonomic correction
- Cervical traction in selected patients without contraindications
- Neural mobilization when appropriate
- Home exercise programme
**Surgical Management**
- Indications progressive neurological deficit severe persistent radicular pain despite appropriate conservative treatment significant structural compression myelopathy or instability
- Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion ACDF
- Cervical disc replacement in selected patients
- Posterior cervical foraminotomy
- Cervical decompression/laminectomy or laminoplasty when indicated
**Conclusion** Early identification of neurological deficits appropriate investigation posture and exercise based rehabilitation and timely surgical referral in progressive or severe cases are essential

--- **2 THORACIC OUTLET SYNDROME**
**Definition** Thoracic outlet syndrome TOS is a group of disorders caused by compression of the brachial plexus and/or subclavian vessels as they pass through the thoracic outlet producing neurological or vascular symptoms in the upper limb
**Types**
- Neurogenic TOS brachial plexus involvement
- Venous TOS subclavian vein involvement
- Arterial TOS subclavian artery involvement
**Causes / Risk Factors**
- Cervical rib or first rib abnormality
- Fibrous bands or abnormal scalene muscles
- Forward head and rounded shoulder posture
- Clavicular/first rib trauma
- Repetitive overhead activity
- Heavy lifting and occupational overuse
**Pathophysiology** Anatomical abnormality or postural dysfunction → narrowing of thoracic outlet → neurovascular compression → neurological and/or vascular symptoms
**Clinical Features**
- Neck shoulder and arm pain
- Paraesthesia numbness and weak grip
- Symptoms aggravated by overhead activity
- Venous type swelling cyanosis heaviness and superficial veins
- Arterial type coldness pallor reduced pulse and ischaemic symptoms
- Possible positive Adson Roos/EAST Wright or costoclavicular manoeuvres
**Investigations**
- X ray of cervical spine/chest for cervical rib
- Doppler ultrasound
- CT angiography or MR angiography for vascular disease
- MRI when structural pathology is suspected
- EMG/NCV in selected neurogenic cases
**Complications**
- Chronic neuropathic pain
- Muscle weakness and wasting
- Venous thrombosis
- Arterial thrombosis or distal embolization
- Limb ischaemia
- Functional disability
**Conservative / Physiotherapy Management**
- Activity modification
- Postural correction
- Scalene and pectoralis minor stretching
- Thoracic mobility exercises
- Deep neck flexor strengthening
- Scapular stabilization
- Breathing exercises
- Ergonomic correction
- Neural mobilization when appropriate
- Avoid prolonged overhead activity and heavy loads on the affected side
**Surgical Management**
- Indications include severe vascular compromise thrombosis progressive neurological deficit significant structural compression or failure of appropriate conservative care
- First rib resection
- Scalenectomy/scalenotomy
- Cervical rib excision
- Fibrous band release
- Vascular reconstruction when required
**Conclusion** Management depends on whether the syndrome is neurological venous or arterial rehabilitation is important in appropriate cases while vascular emergencies require urgent medical treatment

--- **3 VERTEBROBASILAR SYNDROME**
**Definition** Vertebrobasilar syndrome refers to neurological manifestations caused by reduced blood flow or ischaemia in the vertebral and basilar arterial circulation supplying the brainstem cerebellum and posterior cerebral structures
**Causes**
- Atherosclerosis
- Thrombosis or embolism
- Vertebral artery dissection
- Hypertension diabetes and hyperlipidaemia
- Cervical arterial injury or trauma
- Rare vascular abnormalities or compression
**Pathophysiology** Vascular disease → reduced vertebrobasilar blood flow → brainstem/cerebellar ischaemia → neurological dysfunction
**Clinical Features**
- Vertigo and dizziness
- Ataxia and gait disturbance
- Diplopia
- Dysarthria
- Dysphagia
- Nystagmus
- Facial or limb sensory symptoms
- Limb weakness
- Drop attacks or altered consciousness in severe disease
**Red flag presentation** Vertigo associated with diplopia dysarthria severe ataxia weakness or other focal neurological symptoms may indicate posterior circulation ischaemia and requires urgent medical assessment
**Investigations**
- MRI brain
- CT brain when appropriate
- CT angiography
- MR angiography
- Vascular Doppler studies when indicated
- ECG and echocardiography when an embolic source is suspected
- Glucose lipid and coagulation investigations as clinically indicated
**Complications**
- Transient ischaemic attacks
- Posterior circulation stroke
- Permanent neurological deficit
- Dysphagia and aspiration
- Falls
- Loss of consciousness
- Respiratory dysfunction in severe brainstem involvement
- Death in severe stroke
**Conservative / Medical Management**
- Urgent stroke/TIA assessment when suspected
- Antiplatelet treatment when indicated
- Statin therapy when indicated
- Control of blood pressure diabetes and other vascular risk factors
- Smoking cessation and lifestyle modification
**Physiotherapy Management**
- Only after medical stabilization when appropriate
- Balance and coordination training
- Gait training
- Vestibular rehabilitation for suitable patients
- Strengthening and functional retraining
- Fall prevention
- Multidisciplinary management of swallowing problems
**Surgical / Endovascular Management**
- Selected patients may require endovascular treatment
- Angioplasty/stenting in appropriate vascular lesions
- Mechanical thrombectomy for eligible acute ischaemic stroke
- Surgical treatment for selected structural vascular lesions
**Conclusion** Vertebrobasilar syndrome is potentially serious Recognition of posterior circulation warning signs and urgent medical referral are more important than routine musculoskeletal treatment

--- **4 SCALENE SYNDROME**
**Definition** Scalene syndrome is a form of thoracic outlet compression in which the brachial plexus and/or subclavian vessels are compressed within the interscalene triangle formed by the anterior and middle scalene muscles and the first rib
**Causes**
- Scalene muscle hypertrophy or spasm
- Fibrous bands
- Cervical rib
- First rib abnormality
- Poor posture
- Repetitive overhead activity
- Whiplash or other trauma
- Heavy lifting
**Pathophysiology** Scalene tightness or structural abnormality → reduced interscalene space → neurovascular compression → pain paraesthesia weakness and/or vascular symptoms
**Clinical Features**
- Neck and shoulder pain
- Radiating arm pain
- Paraesthesia and numbness
- Weak grip or hand weakness
- Coldness pallor or swelling when vessels are involved
- Tenderness and tightness of scalene muscles
- Restricted cervical movement
**Investigations**
- Clinical examination
- Cervical/chest X ray
- Doppler vascular studies when indicated
- MRI/CT
- EMG/NCV for neurological involvement
- Vascular imaging in suspected vascular TOS
**Complications**
- Chronic pain
- Persistent paraesthesia
- Weakness and wasting
- Vascular compromise
- Thrombosis in vascular cases
- Functional limitation
**Conservative Management**
- Analgesics/NSAIDs when appropriate
- Activity modification
- Scalene stretching
- Postural correction
- Deep neck flexor strengthening
- Scapular stabilization
- Thoracic mobility
- Pectoral stretching
- Breathing exercises
- Neural mobilization when appropriate
**Surgical Management**
- Indications persistent severe symptoms progressive neurological deficit significant vascular compromise or failure of appropriate conservative treatment
- Scalenectomy/scalenotomy
- First rib resection
- Fibrous band release
- Cervical rib excision when present
**Conclusion** Scalene syndrome should be differentiated from other causes of cervicobrachial pain and thoracic outlet symptoms Treatment is initially conservative unless significant neurological or vascular compromise is present

--- **5 COSTOCLAVICULAR SYNDROME**
**Definition** Costoclavicular syndrome is a form of thoracic outlet syndrome caused by compression of neurovascular structures between the clavicle and first rib when the costoclavicular space becomes narrowed
**Causes**
- Drooping shoulders and poor posture
- Clavicular deformity or fracture malunion
- First rib abnormality
- Surrounding muscle tightness
- Carrying heavy loads
- Trauma
- Repetitive shoulder depression
**Pathophysiology** Shoulder depression or structural abnormality → clavicle approaches first rib → costoclavicular space narrows → neurovascular compression → neurological and/or vascular symptoms
**Clinical Features**
- Pain in neck shoulder or arm
- Paraesthesia and numbness
- Weakness and hand fatigue
- Arm heaviness
- Swelling or cyanosis in venous involvement
- Coldness pallor or reduced circulation in arterial involvement
- Symptoms may be reproduced by costoclavicular positioning
**Investigations**
- X ray
- Doppler ultrasound
- CT/MR angiography when vascular disease is suspected
- MRI
- EMG/NCV for selected neurological cases
**Complications**
- Chronic nerve compression
- Weakness
- Venous thrombosis
- Arterial compromise
- Ischaemia
- Functional impairment
**Conservative Management**
- Analgesics and activity modification
- Postural correction
- Scapular stabilization
- Shoulder girdle strengthening
- Pectoral stretching
- Thoracic extension and mobility exercises
- Breathing exercises
- Ergonomic correction
- Avoidance of heavy loads
**Surgical Management**
- First rib resection in selected severe cases
- Decompression of abnormal structures
- Clavicular decompression in selected structural cases
- Vascular reconstruction when required
**Conclusion** The objective is to increase the costoclavicular space reduce neurovascular compression and restore normal shoulder girdle mechanics

--- **6 LEVATOR SCAPULAE SYNDROME**
**Definition** Levator scapulae syndrome is a painful musculoskeletal condition characterized by pain tenderness and increased tension or dysfunction of the levator scapulae muscle commonly associated with poor posture repetitive activity and cervical/scapular dysfunction
**Causes**
- Forward head posture
- Rounded shoulders
- Prolonged sitting
- Poor workstation ergonomics
- Levator scapulae overuse
- Muscle spasm or trigger points
- Whiplash or sudden neck movement
- Cervical spondylosis
- Scapular dyskinesis
- Repetitive overhead activity
**Pathophysiology** Prolonged postural loading or overuse → increased levator scapulae tension → local tenderness/trigger points → pain and restricted cervical/scapular movement
**Clinical Features**
- Pain at the superomedial angle of the scapula
- Neck and upper shoulder pain
- Pain toward the medial scapular border
- Local tenderness and trigger points
- Restricted cervical ROM
- Pain with prolonged sitting
- Symptoms aggravated by cervical rotation or side flexion
**Investigations**
- Usually a clinical diagnosis
- Postural and scapular movement assessment
- Cervical X ray when indicated
- MRI if significant cervical pathology is suspected
**Complications**
- Chronic neck pain
- Recurrent muscle spasm
- Headache
- Reduced cervical ROM
- Scapular dysfunction
- Reduced work tolerance
- Sleep disturbance
**Conservative / Physiotherapy Management**
- Heat or TENS for symptom relief when appropriate
- Soft tissue and manual therapy
- Levator scapulae and upper trapezius stretching
- Pectoral stretching
- Deep neck flexor strengthening
- Scapular retractors lower trapezius and serratus anterior strengthening
- Postural correction
- Ergonomic modification
- Trigger point techniques
- Home exercise programme
**Surgical Management** Surgery is rarely required If symptoms are due to an underlying structural cervical or shoulder disorder treatment is directed toward the underlying pathology
**Conclusion** Most patients respond well to correction of posture muscle imbalance mobility restrictions and ergonomic factors

--- **7 PIRIFORMIS SYNDROME**
**Definition** Piriformis syndrome is a condition in which the sciatic nerve is irritated or compressed by the piriformis muscle in the deep gluteal region producing buttock pain with or without radiating sciatic type symptoms
**Causes**
- Anatomical variation between piriformis and sciatic nerve
- Piriformis hypertrophy or spasm
- Direct buttock trauma
- Prolonged sitting
- Running or repetitive hip rotation
- Overuse
- Poor biomechanics
- Sacroiliac or hip dysfunction
**Pathophysiology** Piriformis overuse/spasm or anatomical variation → sciatic nerve irritation/compression → local inflammation → buttock pain with or without radiating symptoms
**Clinical Features**
- Deep buttock pain
- Pain radiating into posterior thigh
- Sciatic type symptoms
- Paraesthesia or numbness
- Pain aggravated by prolonged sitting
- Tenderness over piriformis
- Pain with resisted hip external rotation
- Pain with piriformis stretching
- Possible reduced hip ROM
**Special Tests**
- FAIR test
- Freiberg sign
- Pace sign
- Beatty manoeuvre
**Differential Diagnosis**
- Lumbar radiculopathy
- Lumbar disc prolapse
- Sacroiliac joint dysfunction
- Hip pathology
- Hamstring pathology
- Spinal stenosis
**Investigations**
- Primarily a clinical diagnosis
- MRI lumbar spine or pelvis to exclude other pathology
- EMG/NCV in selected cases
- Ultrasound in selected cases
- Diagnostic local injection in selected persistent cases
**Complications**
- Chronic buttock pain
- Persistent sciatic symptoms
- Reduced walking and sitting tolerance
- Sleep disturbance
- Reduced athletic performance
- Functional disability
**Conservative / Physiotherapy Management**
- Activity modification and avoidance of prolonged sitting
- Heat/cold or TENS when appropriate
- Piriformis hip rotator and gluteal stretching
- Gluteus maximus and medius strengthening
- Core strengthening
- Neural mobilization when appropriate
- Gait/running biomechanics correction
- Gradual return to sport
- Analgesics/NSAIDs when appropriate
- Selected image guided injection for persistent symptoms
**Surgical Management**
- Rarely required
- Considered after appropriate conservative treatment in severe persistent cases with convincing evidence of sciatic nerve compression
- Piriformis release
- Sciatic nerve decompression
- Correction of associated structural abnormalities
**Conclusion** A careful differential diagnosis is essential because lumbar radiculopathy and other hip/spinal disorders can mimic piriformis syndrome/// CO4 /// ----------------

-- **1 CEREBRAL PALSY**
**Definition** Cerebral palsy is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture causing activity limitation attributed to non progressive disturbances occurring in the developing fetal or infant brain It may be accompanied by disturbances of sensation perception cognition communication behaviour and epilepsy
**Causes / risk factors**
- Prenatal congenital brain malformations intrauterine infections genetic abnormalities maternal diabetes or hypertension and placental abnormalities
- Perinatal prematurity low birth weight hypoxic ischaemic injury intracranial haemorrhage and neonatal seizures
- Postnatal meningitis encephalitis head injury cerebrovascular injury severe hypoxia kernicterus and hypoglycaemia
**Classification**
- Spastic CP hemiplegia diplegia and quadriplegia
- Dyskinetic CP dystonia and choreoathetosis
- Ataxic CP poor balance incoordination and tremor
- Mixed CP combination of motor patterns
**Clinical features**
- Delayed motor milestones
- Abnormal muscle tone spasticity dystonia or hypotonia
- Weakness and poor selective motor control
- Abnormal reflexes and persistence of primitive reflexes
- Abnormal gait and poor balance
- Contractures and deformities
- Hip displacement scoliosis and foot deformities
- Seizures
- Visual/hearing impairment
- Speech communication feeding or swallowing difficulties
- Cognitive or behavioural difficulties in some individuals
**Complications**
- Contractures
- Joint deformities
- Hip subluxation/dislocation
- Scoliosis
- Osteopenia
- Pain
- Reduced mobility
- Epilepsy
- Feeding and respiratory problems
- Reduced independence and participation
**Investigations**
- Neurological and developmental assessment
- MRI brain
- EEG when seizures are suspected
- Hip radiographs when indicated
- Spine radiographs when indicated
- Vision and hearing assessment
- Functional assessment
**Medical management**
- Individualized multidisciplinary management
- Spasticity oral antispastic medications in selected patients
- Botulinum toxin for focal spasticity
- Intrathecal baclofen in selected severe cases
- Antiepileptic medication when required
- Pain feeding constipation bladder nutrition and respiratory management
**Surgical management**
- Tendon lengthening and tendon transfer
- Osteotomy and correction of hip displacement
- Foot reconstruction
- Spinal surgery for severe scoliosis
- Selective dorsal rhizotomy in carefully selected children with severe lower limb spasticity
- Intrathecal baclofen pump in selected severe generalized spasticity
**Physiotherapy management**
- Promote motor development and functional movement
- Positioning and seating for alignment
- Passive/active ROM and stretching
- Strengthening and weight bearing activities
- Postural control and balance training
- Gait training with appropriate aids
- Orthoses when indicated
- Transfer ADL and mobility training
- Respiratory physiotherapy when required
- Home exercise and caregiver education
**Multidisciplinary approach**
- Paediatrician/neurologist
- Orthopaedic surgeon
- Physiotherapist
- Occupational therapist
- Speech and language therapist
- Orthotist
- Psychologist
- Special educator
- Dietitian
- Social worker and rehabilitation physician
**Conclusion** Cerebral palsy is a lifelong condition requiring early individualized and multidisciplinary rehabilitation Management aims to maximize mobility independence participation and quality of life while preventing secondary complications

--- **2 POLIOMYELITIS**
**Definition** Poliomyelitis is an acute viral infectious disease caused by poliovirus primarily affecting motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord and sometimes the brainstem resulting in acute flaccid paralysis
**Causative organism and transmission**
- Poliovirus is an enterovirus of the Picornaviridae family
- Transmission is mainly feco oral through contaminated food and water
- Oral oral transmission may also occur
**Pathogenesis**
- Virus enters through gastrointestinal or respiratory tract
- Replicates in pharynx and intestine
- May enter bloodstream
- In some individuals reaches the CNS
- Motor neurons of anterior horn may be destroyed
- This produces lower motor neuron weakness and flaccid paralysis
**Clinical types**
- Inapparent infection
- Abortive poliomyelitis fever malaise headache sore throat nausea/vomiting
- Non paralytic poliomyelitis meningitic symptoms such as headache neck stiffness and muscle pain
- Paralytic poliomyelitis acute flaccid often asymmetrical paralysis with reduced/absent reflexes
- Bulbar poliomyelitis dysphagia dysarthria respiratory difficulty and cranial nerve dysfunction
**Clinical features**
- Fever fatigue and headache
- Nausea/vomiting
- Muscle pain
- Acute flaccid weakness
- Asymmetrical paralysis
- Reduced muscle tone
- Reduced/absent deep tendon reflexes
- Muscle wasting
- Respiratory and swallowing weakness in severe disease
- Sensation is generally preserved
**Complications**
- Respiratory failure
- Aspiration
- Permanent paralysis
- Contractures
- Joint deformities
- Scoliosis
- Limb length discrepancy
- Osteoporosis
- Gait abnormalities
- Post polio syndrome
**Investigations**
- Clinical neurological examination
- Stool testing for poliovirus
- Throat specimens when appropriate
- CSF examination
- Electromyography
- Nerve conduction studies
- Respiratory function assessment when required
**Medical management**
- There is no specific treatment that reverses established paralytic poliomyelitis
- Supportive care hydration nutrition and pain/fever management
- Respiratory support and assisted ventilation when required
- Airway clearance
- Swallowing management
- Prevention and treatment of complications
**Surgical management**
- Surgery does not treat the acute viral infection
- For residual deformity tendon transfer tendon lengthening osteotomy contracture correction foot reconstruction and spinal surgery for severe scoliosis
**Physiotherapy management**
- Acute positioning gentle passive ROM breathing exercises pressure relieving measures and appropriate splinting
- Avoid excessive exercise of acutely denervated muscles
- Recovery active assisted and gradual active exercise muscle re education and strengthening of useful innervated muscles
- Residual gait training orthoses functional independence and energy conservation
- Post polio syndrome pacing energy conservation appropriate low/moderate exercise and avoidance of overuse
**Prevention**
- Vaccination with IPV and/or OPV according to the applicable immunization programme
- Safe water and sanitation
- Hand hygiene
- Surveillance and outbreak control
**Conclusion** Poliomyelitis can produce permanent motor disability through anterior horn motor neuron injury Supportive medical care prevention of secondary complications physiotherapy orthotic management and reconstructive surgery when necessary are central to rehabilitation

--- **3 SPINAL DYSRAPHISM**
**Definition** Spinal dysraphism is a group of congenital disorders caused by abnormal development and incomplete closure of neural tube and/or vertebral structures producing defects involving the spinal cord meninges vertebrae and overlying tissues
**Classification**
- Open dysraphism neural tissue is exposed or incompletely covered
- Myelomeningocele spinal cord and meninges protrude through a vertebral defect
- Myelocele neural tissue is directly exposed
- Closed dysraphism skin covered defects such as spina bifida occulta meningocele lipomyelomeningocele tethered cord and dermal sinus
**Causes / risk factors**
- Multifactorial origin
- Folate deficiency
- Maternal nutritional deficiency
- Certain maternal medications
- Maternal diabetes
- Genetic susceptibility
- Previous pregnancy affected by neural tube defect
- Environmental factors
**Clinical features**
- Lower limb weakness or paralysis
- Flaccid or spastic paralysis depending on lesion
- Reduced sensation
- Altered reflexes
- Bladder and bowel dysfunction
- Hip dislocation
- Contractures
- Clubfoot and other foot deformities
- Knee deformities
- Scoliosis/kyphosis
- Hydrocephalus
- Chiari II malformation especially with myelomeningocele
- Tethered cord
- Pressure sores
**Complications**
- Hydrocephalus
- Neurological deterioration
- Tethered cord syndrome
- Recurrent urinary tract infection
- Renal damage
- Bowel dysfunction
- Contractures and deformities
- Pressure sores
- Scoliosis
- Reduced mobility
- Psychosocial difficulties
**Investigations**
- Prenatal ultrasound and maternal screening
- Fetal MRI in selected cases
- Postnatal MRI spine
- Ultrasound/CT in selected cases
- Neurological examination
- Urodynamic studies
- Renal function assessment
- Orthopaedic assessment
**Medical management**
- Hydrocephalus management
- Bladder and bowel management
- Prevention of infection
- Skin care
- Nutritional support
- Pain management
- Management of associated neurological problems
**Surgical management**
- Early closure of myelomeningocele to protect neural tissue
- Hydrocephalus ventriculoperitoneal shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy in selected cases
- Tethered cord release when clinically indicated
- Orthopaedic procedures tendon procedures osteotomy foot correction hip procedures and spinal deformity correction
**Physiotherapy management**
- Protect surgical wound and prevent pressure sores
- Proper positioning and gentle ROM
- Facilitate motor development
- Improve head and trunk control
- Strengthen available muscles
- Encourage age appropriate mobility
- Stretching splinting and orthotic management
- Sitting and standing balance
- Gait training when possible
- Wheelchair and transfer skills
- ADL and community mobility training
**Bladder and bowel rehabilitation**
- Timed voiding
- Clean intermittent catheterization when prescribed
- Bowel programme
- Skin care
- Patient and family education
**Multidisciplinary approach**
- Neurosurgeon
- Paediatrician
- Urologist
- Orthopaedic surgeon
- Physiotherapist
- Occupational therapist
- Orthotist
- Rehabilitation physician
- Nurse
- Psychologist and social worker
**Conclusion** Spinal dysraphism can cause neurological orthopaedic and urological disability Early surgical management combined with lifelong multidisciplinary rehabilitation maximizes independence and prevents secondary complications

--- **4 LEPROSY**
**Definition** Leprosy Hansen disease is a chronic infectious disease caused mainly by Mycobacterium leprae primarily affecting the skin peripheral nerves mucosa of the upper respiratory tract and eyes
**Causative organism and transmission**
- Mycobacterium leprae is an acid fast bacillus
- Primarily affects Schwann cells and macrophages
- Transmission is associated with prolonged close contact with untreated infectious disease particularly respiratory droplets
- It is not spread by casual brief contact
**Classification**
- WHO operational classification paucibacillary PB and multibacillary MB
- Ridley Jopling spectrum indeterminate tuberculoid borderline tuberculoid mid borderline borderline lepromatous and lepromatous
**Clinical features**
- Hypopigmented or reddish skin patches
- Definite sensory loss over lesions
- Dry skin and loss of sweating
- Nodules in some forms
- Loss of hair over lesions
- Thickened peripheral nerves with sensory/motor deficit
- Paraesthesia and numbness
- Muscle weakness and wasting
- Foot drop
- Claw hand
- Lagophthalmos
- Recurrent ulcers and burns
**Common nerves affected**
- Ulnar nerve
- Median nerve
- Radial nerve
- Common peroneal nerve
- Posterior tibial nerve
- Facial nerve
**Complications**
- Peripheral neuropathy
- Sensory loss and paralysis
- Contractures
- Claw hand
- Foot drop
- Muscle wasting
- Recurrent ulcers
- Burns and secondary infection
- Corneal anaesthesia and ulceration
- Visual impairment
- Stigma and social/occupational difficulties
**Investigations**
- Complete skin examination
- Sensory testing
- Peripheral nerve examination
- Motor examination
- Slit skin smear when indicated
- Skin biopsy
- Eye examination
- Functional assessment
**Medical management**
- Multidrug therapy MDT is the cornerstone
- Common antileprosy drugs rifampicin dapsone and clofazimine
- Regimen and duration depend on classification and current national/WHO guidance
- Early treatment helps prevent nerve damage and disability
**Management of reactions**
- Type 1 reaction may cause inflammation and acute nerve impairment
- Type 2 reaction may cause fever painful nodules and systemic inflammation
- Corticosteroids and other specialist directed treatment may be required depending on the reaction
**Surgical management**
- Selected nerve decompression
- Tendon transfer for claw hand
- Tendon transfer for foot drop
- Contracture correction
- Reconstructive procedures
- Ulcer management
- Eyelid procedures for lagophthalmos
**Physiotherapy management**
- Assess sensation muscle power ROM deformity skin integrity balance and gait
- Daily skin inspection and protective footwear
- Avoid extreme heat and barefoot walking
- ROM stretching and strengthening of functioning muscles
- Balance and functional training
- Claw hand splinting ROM strengthening and post tendon transfer rehabilitation
- Foot drop AFO gait training and balance training
- Ulcer prevention pressure relief off loading appropriate footwear and education
**Multidisciplinary approach**
- Dermatologist/physician
- Neurologist
- Physiotherapist
- Occupational therapist
- Orthopaedic/plastic surgeon
- Ophthalmologist
- Foot care services where available
- Psychologist and social worker
**Prevention**
- Early diagnosis
- Prompt MDT treatment
- Contact examination/surveillance
